review:
The game is about observing a guy. You don’t control him directly, but instead decide what he’s wearing and what he’s doing by using a card. Basically, it’s like camgirls, but cheaper. 

The gameplay is about making mazes for your ant to run. First you build a deck. Then you use it to construct an obstacle course around a looped unchangeable layout. To get the cards you put in your deck, your hero beats the ever-living crap out of everybody he meets. To get the loot, he does the same.

The cards you play can roughly be divided between three categories: land, that booth boosts the hero and gives you resources for permanent upgrades, mob-spawners, and enhancers of the previous two. The distinction between the categories isn’t clear cut, and cards generally like to interact with each other, which is one of the main gimmicks of the game.
To illustrate, say, you put up a mountain. Nothing happened, just a couple of cowboys are climbing it. Then you put some other mountains around - now it’s a health booster. You put the mountains in a 3x3 square, now it’s one big mountain that gives you a moderate amount of a special resource. And it also spawns bird-women with boobs. Was it because you’re closeted furry? We may never know.
The mobs, just like the cards, interact with each other. Put up a vampire mansion? Now everybody you fight around it sucks. Killed a wandering wolf on an old battlefield? Now kill his ghost. Now kill his ghost’s ghost.

The more cards you play, the more the boss meter fills in. After it’s done, you fight the boss and probably die. After you finish the current loop by dying or by retreating, you start the base building phase. It’s pretty straightforward – you spend your resources, you get the hovels, the hovels give you new cards, new abilities, new bonuses, along with some dialogue. Then you start the loop again.

I’ve skipped through several mechanics, but that’s the gist of it. The game is carried by its stylish presentation and the inherently addictive nature of watching the things you set up play out, somewhat similar to “just one more turn” effect.

Loop Hero’s main flaw is that it’s rather short on content and, because of that, feels rather grindy. It took me 21 hour to unlock almost everything and beat the final boss, and most of the time was spent doing the same things - either grinding the loop while optimizing my deck, or optimizing my deck while grinding the loop. Figuring things out and unlocking new stuff is fun, if sometimes too slow, but it does get old 10-15ish hours in. And due to the mentioned lack of content, there’s no point to use permanent progression to powercreep further once your current strategies start working well enough. 

Overall, I’d say that after the game’s charm is gone, it feels more like a very well-made mobile game built around an addictive gimmick. Now, I ain’t against it, and I think it’s well worth your time for the price - I just wouldn’t go in expecting the world based on all those good reviews.

As a fan of Slay the Spire and strategy games, deck builders and rogue likes in general I thought this game would be right up my street but it turns out not to be a great fit for me. The game lacks meaningful strategic choices and there doesn't seem to be much opportunity to make good or clever plays.

While there are lots of progress paths many of them are very linear. During each run you get gear upgrades, but the choices are often very obvious. I hoped I could steer my "build" into certain areas emphasising particular item stats but often you have a simple choice between the level 6 weapon equipped and the higher damage level 8 weapon you just picked up, regardless of other stats. As you have to be regularly replacing your gear to your current level for it to stay relevant there's little opportunity to push any particular archetype.

The "deck building" element didn't provide much interesting choice for me either. You pick before the run what selection of cards are in the pool to be randomly dropped throughout the run. Some cards synergize with each other but these combos are quickly figured out and for the next 1hr+ you're then confined to this pool. There is a little bit of optimization you can do when placing these tiles during a run but these interactions are quickly figured out.

Combat is all automatic. The combat mechanics aren't explained within the game so there is some experimentation required to discover how certain stats work. The most meaningful choice you do have is when to retire from each run. This push your luck mechanic was initially exciting but with so little influence on your next loop it quickly wore off.

Loop Hero is most akin to a lightweight tower defence game. It lacks opportunities for meaningful choices and player agency. Once you've figured out the basics it's an endless grind. There's nothing here to master that would make it interesting for me long term.
Release an update or DLC, damn it. This is one of my all-time favourite games and I would steal candy from a baby to play more of it.
The best recommendation I can give is the fact that I played the demo for 42 hours before release.

Very fun at first, quickly becomes a time-wasting grind.
Loop Hero is stuck, being neither an ARPG (where the grind process is fun), nor an idle game (where the player can automate the process). This is its ultimate weakness.

There are some accessibility options (fonts, color),  and an interesting narrative.
It is not a bad game, so I recommend it, but with caution.

The world begins as a void, complete nothingness.

Little by little, your quest to rebuild the realm you once inhabited sees your hero remember the way things were. From out of the abyss you run, over and over again. Each time getting closer to understanding how things became so lifeless and bleak. All the while, having an absolute blast, and positively itching for another run.

Loop Hero isn’t simply a retro looking roguelike. It’s a spectacularly packed roguelike/tower defence/city builder/RPG/idle runner/deck builder… I’m honestly having trouble nailing down what exactly the genre of game it is. One thing is for certain though; it’s an expertly crafted mix.

Starting off simply enough, Loop Hero eventually has some incredibly diverse and tight gameplay systems working in tandem. Building a deck of place-able ‘world tiles’ that help and/or hinder your progress through the centre stage ‘loop’, and between runs building further still a sort of base of operations for permanent passive buffs and such… It’s quite a lot to take in. 

But what makes Loop Hero so damn special is when these systems all weave into and through each other, not to mention it all narratively making for some awesome story. I was not expecting such an intriguing and philosophical plot – discussing entropy and the meaning of creation, of all things – in a game that looks perfectly at home sitting among the very first RPGs to hit the PC. It had me thinking about the it a bunch while away from the game, which is always a great plus.

While the visual style is old school, it makes a great case for how awesome pixel art can look if executed properly. Reminiscent of Dungeons & Dragons aesthetics, the sprites for all the beasties and world tiles are excellent. Especially the bosses, simply gorgeous!

Don’t be turned off by the idea of passively watching your hero battle monsters along the trail. The ‘combat’ being hands off took a little to get used to, but once you’re in the mid/end game, battles fly by so rapidly you don’t really take it in. This isn’t a negative though, the hectic pace of it truly elevates the intensity. Making sure there are the right synergies between the loot your hero picks up, and the world tiles you place, is a superb feeling for any would-be tactical strategist.

Loop Hero’s four ‘Acts’, with a bunch of behind the scenes settlement upgrades and bestiary/encyclopedia entries to uncover, gives it a decent shelf life, at around 45 hours for a full playthrough. There’s obviously heaps of potential for repeat runs, trying to optimise your strategy and snag victory with the three different classes.

Managing to get all of these diverse systems into a single game is a phenomenal effort, for a game that appears so devoid of complexity from the beginning.

(There’s also something to be said about the music, which I immediately downloaded after finishing the game, it’s just THAT good. Music composer Blinch has crafted some banger tunes for this game, and if spooky chiptune 16-bit sounds are your jam, you’re gunna love it.)

All in all, other than some light RNG being the difference between trash runs and godly ones, and the obvious eventuality of repetition the core loop will suffer from, there ain’t much to say of flaws in Loop Hero. If any of the genres of game Loop Hero incorporates into the fold interest you, I’d absolutely recommend checking it out.

I love deck building and roguelikes and was excited to try this game. After a while of playing it though, I wanna say this one just ain't for me.

I do wanna give the game props for a few things. First off, The presentation is amazing. The graphics consist of beautiful pixel art that is very vibrant yet also visually cohesive. The game features a limited color palette and it's impressive what they've managed to pull off without compromising quality. The chiptune music is also hits hard and fits well with the environment of the game.

The game was also pretty interesting and addictive for the first 2 chapters for me. I enjoyed the unique premise of building a path where I have to carefully place tiles that isn't brutal enough to kill my hero but challenging enough to get good loot so they can sustain themselves with the scaling difficulty over time.

Around chapter 3 though is where the grind started to dawn on me. After you figure out the right cards to take with you and how to optimally place them, then you've essentially reached the skill ceiling of the game. The game is not difficult mechanically nor is the strategy of picking which gear to equip and when/where to place certain tiles hard to figure out.

I think the devs figured this out and so to give the game some more longevity, they scaled the health/damage numbers of the enemies in the end game. The player then needs to grind for upgrades to their base and supplies to boost their own numbers to win. Conceptually this is fine and many games do this, e.g. looter shooters, but the gameplay itself stagnates. 

Sure the first 10 hours of gameplay or so are novel, but after excitement dies down, you get bored of repeatedly watching automated battles and clicking and dragging tiles. Your reward for doing 1-2 hours are rng items that very incrementally increase your strength. We're talking about +1% health bonuses that you'll want to stack 100+ of to really feel the effect.

After I beat chapter 3, I had no more motivation to keep playing. Some people may enjoy looking up what to farm and how to farm it. But for me, the gameplay loop is not fun enough to keep going.

I enjoyed this game, I had a great time learning what to do and how to progress. The game’s main strength is how it introduces new concepts over the course of the game. It doesn’t rush everything and drip feeds you new abilities and content to keep you interested.

Loop Hero is quite the unique game, to describe it as a roguelike would be inaccurate. To describe it as a dungeon crawler would be better but still not quite accurate. To describe it as an RPG manager would be the best way of describing it, a game I would consider closest to this is Darkest Dungeon. The components of the game are managing your trinkets and the campsite, and succeeding in expeditions. When you do an expedition you are collecting resources and if you can defeating the boss of that chapter. An expedition is the main part of the game, your character walks around in a loop while you place down tiles that have an effect on the character or what the character might encounter. Using resources you then build buildings at your campsite. These buildings unlock new abilities or tiles which you can encounter in expeditions. You pick what kind of tiles you will have at the start of an expedition and some tiles have special interactions when placed next to other tiles. Also you can have it on in the background while doing other things. Oh yeah, the games can be short as 15 minutes or drag on for 14 hours, when you beat the boss of a chapter you can keep playing. You can get an absolute ton of resources for doing this which will make you easily beat the game.

The games aesthetics are excellent. Good music, art direction and story. One of the reasons I plugged away at this game was to find out why the world was being unmade and who the hell this skeletal mage is, don’t worry this is literally the start of the game, this isn’t spoiler territory. It’s not going to go into any sort of moral depth but the curiosity of why is enough for me to keep at this game.

The other part of the game is the numbers, Loop Hero is a very math heavy game. You will be comparing a lot of numbers and coming to a decision on what items you should use in a game. This is at first very confusing, something I will address now. There is a rarity system in the game but it works on two levels, the colours are grey, blue, yellow, orange. Grey only gives one stat ability, Orange gives four. However the magnitude of these abilities is a little random and therein lies the second scale of rarity in how good these stats are. Usually the item has a high level compared to what loop of the expedition you are on. The numbers are something you get used to over the course of the game.

One thing I have neglected to mention is combat, simply because that is not your job. Your character will do that bit automatically, they select their targets and begin hacking away at it until it dies. You are a weird spectator in your own game, all you can do is change the environment to benefit your character or make item picks in your characters favour. The weird thing is that this works as a form of gameplay, at no point did I feel detached from my character. The result of an expedition always felt as if it was down to you, the player.
In terms of weaknesses of this game, what I will say is that this game gets repetitive, it literally says it in the title. Thankfully the change ups in the gameplay keep the game fresh for a long time. Once you beat the final boss however there isn’t much left to play for, unless you’re getting achievements. The other problem is more outside of the game where I find the fanbase is a little meta-obsessed. Like any game involving cards there are going to be people out there who will tell you the correct way to play the game, exploration of other ideas is dumb and you’re a stupid person for doing it. Considering I beat the final boss six times without looking at guides, you can easily not look at the community and eventually you’ll beat the boss in your own way. Exploration of the game mechanics is a part of Loop Hero, you’re punished for getting things wrong but there is very much the atmosphere of ‘try again’. 

Overall I would recommend this game to people who have played Darkest Dungeon. It’s an easier game and is quicker to complete. I would recommend it to people who play combat based classic RPGs, a lot of familiar mechanics plus this game is on cruise control. I would also say the game is somewhat casual, it doesn’t require lightning fast reflexes and can be paused. If I scaled it in my top 100 it is in the 90’s, not a classic but an interesting niche little game worthy of a good play.

However, it overstays its welcome and becomes way too grindy starting from Act III. But the first ~20 hours I had a blast.
The game is great fun, but it feels incomplete. The developers promised to add a bunch of stuff after the game launched and then they just didn't

Game is extremely well made and super addictive, but that doesn't make it fun. Kind of like how a song you hate can still be catchy and get stuck in your head. I think way too many people get the idea that if they played a game for 5+ hours that must mean they enjoyed it and then try to rationalize how it was actually fun after the fact.

I played for basically 7 hours straight caught in a trance of repeating the same mundane actions over and over again before I finally just had to stop and ask myself "wtf am i doing?". Would not recommend unless you just want to kill time and have nothing else to do, but I would strongly suggest you put your limited time on earth engaged with something slightly more challenging or interesting.

This game is great, worth every penny.
Although the full game is live, I see a lot of potential for updates in the future.

Pros:
-Simple system to pick up
-pixel graphics
-multiple classes playable which adds depth to play styles 
-multiple builds available for decks and classes
-resource system to build up camp for roguelike attributes for future runs
-chapters allow for harder runs with bonus loot
-enemies are very balanced in the way they become stronger every loop and in further chapters
-statistics feature keeps track of pretty much all your stats 

Cons:
-crafted items have clear S-F tiers where lower tiers don't really benefit you much
-special tiles like blood path, hungry grove, etc are found by trial and error. Although it encourages players to try new things, could add hints in encyclopedia to help players find the combos
-there's no way to pause a run and later come back to it, so if you are on a very long run, you have to retreat before closing 

Simply put, this is a great roguelike which will steal hours of your life and make you say "maybe one more loop" so many times you'll forget to eat.
Highly recommend this game and look forward to updates to come!

It's addictive as hell, but is it fun? After about 13 hours (I know, virtually no time at all compared to some of you) I'd say... no. My desire to keep playing wasn't related to fun at all. It just has the perfect formula to keep you trying for "one more loop". 
The base (your permanent upgrades) is cumbersome, and acquiring the materials is part of the addiction. You want to see what new cards you get after grinding for those materials, right? Once you get those new cards it's going to start being "fun", isn't it? Nope.
It's just a big grind. The entire game is one grind after another, which is appealing for some but definitely not for me. It just feels like a mobile game without the microtransactions.
The visuals are great and the story is mildly interesting, but I'd still say give it a skip.

Game starts out great but quickly falls apart after you get some unlocks going.
The game is completely unbalanced and leads to specific strats, stats, and cards being strictly better than all others in all cases. This quickly makes the gameplay fairly predictable and boring. It also makes getting RNG screwed because you don't get any gear with the good stats less than fun. 

The game has no tooltips and does not explain the vast majority of its mechanics. The descriptions it does have are poor at best or outright wrong at worst.  

These two issues combine in some terrible ways. For example, upon beating a boss you are given a choice of 4 rewards: 3 are things that read like weak permanent buffs; the 4th is a cache of mats. The 4th is really small and doesn't look like a choice though, so you're unlikely to click it.  So you will likely choose one of the 3. Turns out they're not permanent buffs as a reward for beating a level, but incredibly bad skills that are now added to your level up pool. You just made your character permanently weaker by polluting your level up skill pool with garbage.

The number of interesting/useful interactions seems high at first, but turns out to be shallow when most combo tiles are basically just "slightly better variant" or tile or "place X number of tiles and receive punishment tile". 

For a game that seems to want you to grind and have any semblance of length to it, the games rewards for grinding are abysmal. You can continue to upgrade your town past the basic unlocks for absolutely pitiful rewards at the cost of ridiculous amounts of resources. There is the supply depot, where you can get artifacts that can permanently buff your char if you equip them, but they are pitifully weak unless you stack dupes, rare, expensive, and completely RNG.

Finally, the beginning of a run will always be the same, slow and incredibly boring. Walking around fighting slimes and hoping for cards to drop to make things faster and more interesting.  Starting a run is boring and sucks.

Once you start to understand the game, it falls apart.

This is a great example of a nicely done and completely original indie game. You don't need to have AAA level graphics or a story that can compete with Hugo/Nebula winning books. To be honest this game has neither, as graphics are below mediocre even by retro pixel art standards and story is nonexistent except some short dialogues. BUT the gameplay concept is so unique that you don't even care about those. I can describe the game as "reverse TD rogue-lite RPG" if it makes any sense :D 

If you decide to try it, do not forget to edit game speed from "variables.ini" inside game folder as the default 2x option is still a bit slow. "game_speed=240" feels fine (default is 60)

A fresh compelling take on rogue likes. Loop Hero doesn't do a good job of explaining all the mechanics in detail, and that's intentional. You're thrown into chaos looping endlessly while you struggle to build something from nothing. Loop Hero combines deck building, town building, and other strategic elements seamlessly with a completely idle combat system. 

In Loop Hero you mainly go on expeditions, this is where the looping happens. Expeditions feature a randomly generated road for your hero to automatically loop around whilst fighting monsters and farming precious resources to expand your town. Your town is part of a progression system that helps you on future expeditions by expanding and upgrading it. While your hero is looping you have a few strategic decisions to make such as placing tiles and deciding what is the best combination of gear to equip.

Explaining the game further however doesn't do it justice, Loop Hero took me by surprise and is best experienced by playing it for yourself, so that is what I recommend you do.

Way more fun than I expected an autobattler to be. It's far from mindless and probably has sort of a medium-level of depth to it.

You choose what will be in your pool of cards though it's sort of a stretch calling them cards really. They become structures or monsters you place on the path of the level. The goal is basically to make a level that causes you to fight as many monsters as you can handle, but not too many, to stay strong enough to keep up with the increasing difficulty. It's pretty unique and if you don't pay attention you'll make game ending choices.

Every song is a bop, and the pixel art actually looks good instead of like zork. It looks like final fantasy 1 art except a step up.

There's a decent amount of variation mainly through deck creation and character class.  The biggest problem is probably that its systems promote grinding, and the amount of resources needed to make progress is not light. Unsurprisingly like in many modern games, the 'content' or playtime is severely padded by high resource costs. It's also a bit annoying to unlock the classes and takes a long time before you can play them. When building your town between runs, a stupid lack of transparency will probably make you need to destroy buildings and move them somewhere else wasting even more resources.

All of the permanent meta progression takes super long. They're fun unlocks that really change what's going on, but it's too much. Surprisingly good game, just sullied a bit by padding via resource costs.

This game is great and totally worth the $15. It's a cross between an idle game, a deckbuilder and a strategy game. Maybe more, I think if you tried to list off all this game's genres and influences you'd have a book, or at least a pamphlet. If this game seems interesting to you or your friends are telling you to play it...

TRY OUT THE DEMO.

The demo is the entire first chapter with some limitations, but it definitely gives you plenty of playtime to decide if you'll enjoy the game (you probably will.) The devs seem to be updating frequently to polish the game and fix bugs, so right out of the gate I'm confident this game will see plenty of content in the coming months. I have 60 hours into Loop Hero so far and it's been out less than a week, there are still about 8 achievements I need to get and a TON of builds I wanna try out, this game has great replayability for people that like to try out different combinations and character builds.

Let's get the genre of this game out of the way first. It more or less is a pseudo idle game. 

The player controls what is placed on the map, and what items the Hero equips to adjust your stats, but after that point in an adventure at least, the game will play itself. For some this may not be compelling. For me, this is relaxing and fun as the game isn't a high pressure hack and slash.

Other things to say about the game is that the game does have "rouge lite" elements of you building up your camp to unlock different abilities and permanent buffs as you go along (kinda like idle games again) in between adventures.

The story is fairly well written though the plot may become a bit obvious at a certain point, but there are still a few twists within.

The soundtrack is fantastic for this game. I have had the song entitled "Loop Blues" stuck in my head for over 2 weeks now, it's that much of a banger in my opinion.

If you don't mind what *is* essentially a type of idle game, Loop Hero is well worth picking up, and I would reccomend it if people were to ask about it.

As I just got all the achievements, I decided to summarize my impressions.

Loop Hero is an amazing game and I had a very enjoyable experience with it. Although, not everyone would appreciate it. While reading negative reviews, I clearly understood why some people were frustrated with this game, but those points that dissatisfied them are actually what made this game amazing for me.

First of all, Loop Hero is indeed an idle game. Well, it kind of is. There is one big difference between «classical» idle games and Loop Hero. And the difference is that you are painting the world you are going to idle. The process of filling up the map is mesmerizing, and there are a lot of different ways you can complete another run. Some are mentioned grinding. I didn't really notice that. Every run I tried to experiment with decks and different terrain placement and not once did I have a feeling that I force myself to replay something in order to gather resources.

Another thing I’d like to address is the sound in this game. The music is great, the effects are really plausible, and I like how every character has its own well-selected sound of voice substitute. But right on the main screen, there are sound options where you can turn it all off. Why would you do that? Because [b]this game is just perfect for those who like to listen to podcasts while playing.[/b]

Although there are a lot of possibilities, they are not endless. I spent 60+ pleasant hours in Loop Hero and there is not much left for me to do, except, maybe, summoning hidden bosses. The game is very much completable, it has a moderate level challenge, and completionists could have the great feeling of 100%ing while spending a reasonable amount of effort.
I personally would definitely recommend the game, even for the full price.

A huge thanks to the developers and I hope to hear about Loop Hero 2 soon.

The idea is great and execution is interesting but this game has a MASSIVE issue : Victory is obtained by farming.

You can place your cards the best way possible, be lucky with your loot and gear and you will absolutely fail that level because you were supposed to unlock a building in your town that give you access to some new cards that give you what you need to win.

Building are obtained by spending ressources. You gain some in levels and you ONLY retain 30% of these if you fail the level. So you just start levels, farm ressources, leave before you get killed, upgrade your base when you can, rinse and repeat until you obtain the building that will unlock that one card to help you. You realize that far after the refund timer.

As a result, the game is padded massively with boring grind. For the comparison's sake, imagine Slay the Spire: but you need to lose 30 runs on purpose to obtain the basic cards you need to win your first run with.
It's like the devs realized the game was only 5 hours long, so instead of having some interesting 5 hours, they padded it with a 40 hours long grindfest.

It's quite a shame, the idea of the game is great and quite addictive, but I can't recommend it due to that.

What an interesting game. I sunk alot of time into it, and I must say, it's one of the most addictive games on the market at the moment. That being said, it's weird.

The difficulty requires experimentation to play around with, and at a certain point, one begins to figure out the builds they like. The obtaining of resources is time consuming, and serves as a grind, but the main game is fun enough where I never really had an issue with it. Easily the most interesting mechanic is deciding whether or not to loop again, and the general risk management, as resources to improve long term are on the line. The real customization comes in the deckbuilding, and figuring out the sort of setup the character is looking for. 

The pacing's interesting. Early on the game's quite fun, but after the first 13 hours it slows down. That being said, the lull is regrettable, as I think the second half of the game is quite strong. The game becomes far more fun once the warehouse is available, as it provides permanent buffs, allowing for an entertaining power snowballing. 

Four Quarters put a lot of effort in and it shows. The games brimming with polish, and the spriting/worldbuilding is fantastic. I love seeing unknown teams strike it big, and they're doing quite well via word of mouth.

That being said, the gameplay's odd. Micromanaging the game is often boring, as the fighting is done for you, but you can rarely leave the hero looping and idle. It's in a weird crossroads between an idle game, and a standard game, and even after 60 hours, I couldn't tell which it wanted to be. 

I definitely recommend Loop Hero, unless you despise grinding in games. For me, it scratched an itch I love scratching, but I can understand why someone might be annoyed with the time it takes up.

I think this is probably the biggest love/hate relationship I have ever had with a game...

I usually don't like doing this, but this is a case where I feel I should give this game the thumbs down, despite the fact I do play and... sort of enjoy this game - mostly to balance out the fact it's already currently very positively received.

To try to put my very conflicted feelings towards this game in as few words as possible, my issue with this game is that it is an amazing and unique idea in theory - but when you actually sit down and play the game it's very dull, repetitive, and slow paced. You'll still find some enjoyment from the pure satisfaction of growing a little bit stronger with each run every time, but honestly, I think the flaw I cannot get past with this game is the absurdly grindy nature of it.

---
| GRINDING
---
The most fun part of this game is just the satisfaction you get from making progress, but the progression is slower than most microtransaction-ridden mobile games, which is especially confusing for a game that doesn't even have microtransactions. It would often take about 8-10 full runs each lasting around half an hour just to get ONE more damn building, and ultimately after all that effort, the benefits would often be as trivial as "oh, now your health potions heal 7% of your health instead of 6%". I can only guess the developers were worried the game isn't long enough? It technically does only have 4 "levels" (unless there's some secret post-game content I'm not aware of), but I honestly feel this would have been much better off as a short and replayable experience, than the absolute slog it is right now to inflate the playtime required to beat it.

---
| RESOURCES
---
Beyond the grinding being ridiculously tedious, every resource in the game required to make any permanent progress has its own special conditions for acquiring them. This is a fine idea, and most resources are obtained through reasonable enough methods - defeat these kinds of enemies to get this, walk through these kinds of tiles to get that - that sort of thing. One very important material needed for most buildings and upgrades in the game though, are orbs of expansion, and the game never tells you how to get them. I checked the encyclopedia and found that no enemies or tiles in the game would give you them, and when looking at the material itself it told me all I had to do was fight multiple enemies at once to obtain it. I then proceeded to do about 5 runs spamming as many enemies as possible into single fights, and at the end of all of them I had gotten 0 orbs of expansion. That's because the limit to the amount of enemies on a tile is 4, and to get orbs of expansion you need to fight groups of 5 enemies (game says 4 works, but I never got one orb from 4-enemy fights, and even with 5 you only have a % chance of getting ONE orb). So how the hell does that work? You have to get a tile with 4 enemies, and then have a nearby building which has some sort of gimmick to add enemies onto an already existing fight to get the fifth enemy. I had to look up guides to figure this out, and even once I started using the best strategy the community had found for grinding these orbs, it still took hours just to get enough for the tiniest of incremental upgrades. This is both extremely unintuitive to figure out, and extremely unfun to do - but you need those incremental upgrades to have a chance at the later boss fights, so get grinding.

---
| GAMEPLAY
---
I like the idea that because you are building the world, you control the enemies that spawn, the resources you'll earn, and to some extent the equipment you'll get throughout a run - however, other than that, the game plays itself entirely. No targetting options for attacks, no movesets for your character, and not even any activated abilities - I can understand maybe wanting the battles to go mostly automatically, but I'm honestly kind of baffled that as far as I've played, this game just doesn't have any way to interact with a battle as it is happening at all.

Of course, the equipment you choose over the course of a run, and the cards you build your Deck with are going to have an effect on the outcome of your battles, but if say you realise "oh I'm a little low on health, and before the next loop I have one more big fight coming up" you genuinely can't do anything most of the time but just watch your character walk blindly into their death. Health potions? You're not allowed to use them manually, the game decides when to use them automatically. Activate some kind of ability to help you? As I said, you don't get any, the only effects you get in this game are passives or one-time use abilities that trigger automatically when the game decides. Play a Card in your Hand? What are you going to play? The vast majority of cards have little to no impact on their own, and also often take a long period of time to give their benefits. The only Card in the entire game that can really save you there I have seen is Oblivion, the one that just deletes everything including enemies on a tile - but you can only get so many of those.

It feels like most runs of this game are just rolling the dice, seeing if the game randomly decides to give you the equipment you need to win this game, and if not - tough luck, go again for the 783rd attempt of doing the exact same thing. It feels to me that for the point in the game I'm at, the only viable strategies are:
1. Attack speed spam with Rogue until you kill so fast nothing gets a chance to hit you (I went infinite twice with this strategy, but you gotta get lucky with equipment for it to work, unfortunately)
2. Attack speed spam with Necromancer to summon a ludicrous amount of skeletons (more consistent, but less likely to scale well into late-game in my experience)
And while these strategies were fun at first, it feels like they're the only strategies in the game that really work even over 50 hours into it. Every time I've thought of trying out a different Deck, the new Deck has been vastly inferior to those 2 Decks, so every game ends up being the same. If I was at least progressing at a reasonable rate, I may have been able to stomach that, but that's just it - I'm not progressing at reasonable rate. I'm spending hours and hours just to get 1% bonuses to certain stats and it just feels like... Why am I playing this game anymore?

---
| CONCLUSION
---
I realised that I spent more of my time playing this game feeling bored or frustrated with all the grinding than actually enjoying it, but that I kept pushing through that for a long time because the initial idea had captivated me so much that I felt like I couldn't write this game off until I'd completed it. I kept thinking this will get better soon, I kept thinking I'll probably like it by the end - and maybe I still will, I still plan to at least finish this game at some point, but I'm no longer in a rush to do it. Taking a moment to step back and realise that I have now spent over 50 hours on this game, and that I only really enjoyed the first 5 or so hours of that, and spent the rest of those hours pushing through because "surely it gets better, right?" has really put in perspective for me why I think I have to give this game the thumbs down despite how much I love the concept - and despite how much I want this to be good.

All that being said, I did say I don't think this is an outright bad game, and believe it or not, I do still stand by that - I just think if you want to play this game to completion, you have to go into it with a certain mindset to enjoy it. Since every run drags on for so long while you have very little control over the outcome of it, this game is much more enjoyable as a sort of "background game" to play while listening to something else or just trying to unwind while doing something to keep you a little busy.

This game is a total brain teaser and a brilliant merge of an RPG and deckbuilding. 

What truly hooked me was the constant sense of exploration.  Every loop offered an opportunity to experiment with new cards, to try out fresh strategies to conquer the path and break the cycle.  Would adding a swamp next to the goblin camp create a deadlier (and more rewarding) encounter?  Would placing a vampire mansion near the hero's starting point be a strategic masterstroke or a recipe for disaster?  The possibilities were endless, and the thrill of discovering a powerful new combo or witnessing the effects of your environmental manipulation was immensely satisfying.

Thankfully, the minimalist interface never gets in the way of the strategic depth.  Everything is understandable and easy to use, which is crucial for a game that relies on experimentation and quick decision-making.  A complex interface could have easily become an insurmountable hurdle, turning the strategic dance into a frustrating exercise in menu navigation. The game strikes a perfect balance, allowing players to focus on the core gameplay loop without unnecessary clutter.

It is a unique and captivating experience, but it might not be for everyone.  The meditative gameplay and slow drip-feed of story might not resonate with all players.  Some nights you'll find yourself staring down the business end of a boss monster, questioning the repetitive nature of the loop.  However, for those who enjoy strategic depth disguised in a deceptively simple package, and who find satisfaction in slowly unraveling a mystery, this game offers a journey like no other.  

Lore?
No, just no.

Is it worth the money?
While the replayability factor might be limited for some, the initial experience and strategic depth make it a worthwhile purchase.

Is it enjoyable?
For majority of the gamers, I would suppose.

Will I ever play it again?
Unlikely.

I wanted to like this game a lot because of the retro fantasy aesthetic. The idea of building the world around you and having these realistic interactions that affect stats/gameplay is fascinating and definitely got me hyped in my early hours. There is some pretty great world building to go along with this too, and I love the dialogues because they help set all that up.

Where the game falls apart for me is in the actual rouge-like elements. Specifically in how repetitive it gets so quickly. I found myself doing the same things over and over again, getting bored of using the same cards and builds because it was what worked without much feeling of forward progress. 

For example, the only class that I've been able to complete runs with any degree of regularity is the warrior. Despite unlocking two other classes, it just seems way more powerful, reliable, and easy to use. Maybe there are cards I would have been able to get later on that work better with the rogue and necromancer, but I don't really know that for sure because you can't view specific details about the tech tree unlocks later down the line. 

Perhaps I might be able to see that one of the next buildings I can build unlocks the "forest" card. Great, what does it do? Does it synergize with one of the other classes somehow? Don't know. I don't even know how to unlock that building, because the game shows me little symbols without names or tooltips for the resources needed to unlock it. I've never seen those symbols before though and they don't seem to correspond to any of the types of resources I've been picking up. None of my cards are capable of making a resource with that symbol and I don't even know what that symbol means because I can't scroll over it to view a tooltip of some kind telling me how I can get it. Even when I spend a lot of hours grinding to unlock a building that supposedly allows me to trade books to unlock codex entries, all it does is unlock flavor text for already discovered things, not new information. 

The opaqueness of these mechanics really kills my motivation to make forward progress because I'm bored of doing the same thing for 10 hours and I have no idea when its going to get better. It also sucks loosing a run, and therefore a bunch of resources, because you suddenly died. Without being able to control the battles directly, the only control you have is in what cards you place, what gear you equip, and what talents you take. But all of that is subject to both RNG (in terms of what you get) and also varies wildly in balance. Some cards/stats/talents are total garbage while others are auto-takes. 

There just isn't enough variety, and a lot of these systems are pretty shallow. Like you're just getting +7% more attack speed or something most of the time. It doesn't make decisions interesting and tactical. Like obviously I'm going to take +7% attack speed over +5% attack speed every time. Its very Diablo-esque in that its about scaling your numbers to get bigger without really making very interesting moment-to-moment decisions. For example, maybe I could get an item that adds possibility of lightning damage to my weapon, and also a talent that says whenever I deal lightning damage, it stuns the enemy for 1 second. An environmental card effect could then say stunned enemies take extra damage or something. This is how you do synergy in an interesting way, but its more complex to implement, and it feels like the developers kinda just didn't want to do all that. 

I think what they wanted to make was an idle mobile game where you really don't do much and don't have much control over anything, because that's what this game is. Its repetitive and the RPG systems are very shallow, even for an RPG lite. It has painfully slow progression and a major lack of variety. 

If you like an endless grind of collecting random resources because I said so and making numbers bigger then this game might be interesting for you, but I like something with more depth. And sure, maybe it gets better later, but I've already played 10 hours. I beat a boss and I'm just bored now because the prospect of doing it all over again with the same setup but harder just isn't appealing to me.

There is a lot of positive feedback here, this is going to cover why I don't recommend it. 

The first 12-15 hours of this game is *absolutely stellar*, but then the cracks start to show. As runs get longer and longer, you realize you have less and less control over what determines a good run from a bad run: the distribution of cards that determine what you can build is randomized (though I suspect it is massaged), so you may only see a copy or two of a given card within a run while you drown in a card you only need two of. As the variety of cards increases during the game, it becomes harder to pin down exactly what is worth trying. Do I just need to keep trying this combination, or should I change it? Some building pattern synergies repeat, others do not, and you start to waste more and more time looking for interesting combinations (if you don't look them up online, which is how I've played). Some cards are really important, others have extremely limited interactions. What's worth your time? There are some hints, but there are few opportunities to build on what you've learned.

Gear and leveling perks are all luck dependent as well. You do need to make intelligent gear choices, but you may also never get the gear you need.

The game's "clock" is determined by building tiles. In many ways I wish the game was balanced around a fixed number of loops rather than such a vacuous time suck of arbitrarily placing the last tile to trigger the boss fight. The game is very good at keeping you playing, it's incredibly well designed in many respects. I would keep playing if the grind involved in beating it was fun, but after a point there aren't new things to easily unlock, and the grind of the game becomes much more real.

This is a very engaging experience, but I wish the design had just decided to be something to finish with less friction, leaving some secrets to return to rather than trying to push you to grind through the final stretch of resource collection and building. I don't care about replay here, but if it's not asking for replay value, I want the end of this game to sparkle like the beginning, and it doesn't.

I finished the first two bosses, and I've been playing with the final class, and then switching things around. The design starts to feel sloppy compared to it's mysterious and sharpened self that you first encountered, gently nudging you to make the right choices with great music, a compelling story, and wonderful visuals to keep you tuned in. I'm almost done with the village tech tree, but I don't really want to grind any more. The music is starting to get too repetitive.

I was looking forward to seeing the end of this, but I don't think that I'm going to. The fact I don't want to finish it makes me feel less good about the time I had spent with it. 

This game is completely worth the money, but I don't think it's worth your time.

Cool concept, but there's some big problems that killed the game for me.

1. The use of language is very sloppy. Sometimes +HP means healing, sometimes it means increasing your max HP. Trial and error is the only way to figure it out. One trait says +1 HP per trophy held, but it's actually per trophy gained, which is a huge difference. Plenty more examples exist. In a game that's almost entirely about optimization, this is just not excusable.

2. Lack of meaningful options. The balance is all over the place, so you frequently don't have any real choice to make. You take in the cards that are the most useful, and pick the perks that are the most useful. It's not too hard to figure out, and it just becomes rote after that.

3. Grindiness. Upgrading the town requires a lot of resources, which are mainly obtained by running the highest chapter you can reliably beat. Coupled with a slow game speed, this becomes tedious quickly. 

There's obviously plenty of good points to the game (art and music, cool atmosphere to the story), and I don't know that most would be as frustrated by the negatives as I am. That said, I didn't really enjoy it, so I don't recommend it.

Interesting take on the RPG/Rogue-lite genre. Eschews combat choice completely (fights are all automatic) in favour of emphasising resource management and equipment optimisation. This does put it dangerously close to idle game territory, but the fast pace of each expedition keeps the player active and entertained.

The main drawback is that after while, the game begins to feel like a grind. Earning some of the rarer materials required to expand your camp (a fairly linear task taking place between each expedition) can take quite a long time. Certain rare orbs may only drop once in a 20 minute round, and when 10 or more are required to build a new structure or upgrade an existing structure, the game begins to feel rather tedious.

There are three distinct classes which keep things varied, but all three are unlocked fairly quickly, and once you have identified optimal builds for each class not much changes from run to run. Rogue-lites are all about repetition, and this is where Loop Hero starts to fall down. By removing combat from the equation, each new run ends up a scavenger hunt, waiting and hoping that the ideal loot will drop.

That said, it took me a good 25 hours to get to the point where things started to feel tedious. I enjoyed the game, and although I doubt I will ever finish it I reckon it's fun enough to be worth a play.

In Loop Hunter you play as a cosmic Bob Ross, painting the endless void to life with a variety of horrors, thugs and beasts while a valiant hero marches in circles and sometimes they even survive to get back home.

Hold on, just wait a minute and let me explain why that's amazing.

You see, some huge jerk of a Lich blew up reality. The only way to get it back - it seems - is to piece-by-piece 'remember' it into existence. "Oh, I remember what a tree looks like" and bam, there's your forest. Unfortunately the more you remember, the more the world is populated by people who, well, aren't generally very friendly. As the dutiful hero dispatches them (whether they want to or not) they gain XP, new equipment, and you outfit them so they can withstand the eventual horror of battling to the death with the universe-consuming Lich.

Naturally one would assume this fantastic premise would involve hurling galaxies like throwing stars, but in reality combat is a rather mundane affair. It's not really the focus and you have no direct control over it.

Instead the focus is on splattering your void with proud mountains, dense battlefields, oppressed hamlets and, of course, a happy little tree right over there. This determines what sorts of enemies spawn, what unique effects occur, and sometimes even what allies come to your aid. It's all great and good to try to make things as easy as possible but when you finally come up against the Lich, well... Do you think that little dinky +1 sword is going to cut it against a dude whose body has turned into galaxies? Not so much.

With that in mind: both you and your foes will die. A lot. When you die - or win, or run away - you return to the budding cluster of strangers huddled around a campfire and terrified of leaving its preserving light. If they leave they may end up vanishing, forgotten, and lost in the void where nothing remains the same for long. The hero uses resources they collect from their journey to help these people and, in turn, the people help the hero. Sometimes it's through potions, other times through training, and occasionally even through direct fire support. Eventually they may even document your encounters, writing down little bits of information and lore that you otherwise wouldn't have guessed at. Some of the lore is quite good, too. In short: fight for them and they'll fight for you - in their own, small ways.

Then the hero heads back out and "remembers" an entirely new world filled with different clusters of enemies and, hopefully, this time doesn't trip up at the finish line for the sixtieth time.

For those who don't know (and I didn't before buying this game) the "loop" is a literal thing in this game.  The world has been blown away by some malfeasance by some unknown evildoer, and you're somehow the only thing left.  You start to remember bits and pieces of stuff (in the form of cards) which you place down on the grid around the looping road and more stuff comes into being.  This makes you remember even more stuff and suddenly you've got visitors at your campfire who seem to remember seeing you leave and are delighted to see you return.

Each time you pass the campfire you're allowed to stop and take a break and you get to keep everything you've earned through your trials and tribulations.  You could also try to escape mid-loop and you'd lose 30% of everything or you could keep going until you die at which point you only get to KEEP 30% of everything... Or something close to that since I can't remember the exact percentages and I can't be bothered to go back and look.

You start each "expedition" barehanded and under-dressed for the occasion, but as you defeat slimes and other enemies you find swords, shields, rings, and armor that you can use to boost your stats and add some new effects.  Some items will increase attack, defense, or may add to your ability to evade attacks or counter when attacked.  You might also get a vampiric ability from them which means each attack returns some hit points, or you may get a more passive health ability that heals you a little at a time.  There's a ton of other abilities but at first this is what you'd focus on for your stats.

Also different tiles placed on or near the road will produce new enemies for every day (or series of days) that go by.  Some tiles may cause  your enemies to be swallowed up when they're almost dead and some tiles may cause them to change into ghosts after you kill them requiring you to kill the ghosts (and maybe even the GHOSTS of the ghosts).  

Also while you're fighting and placing tiles, you'll find materials that won't be useful really until you get enough to lump them into something better.  A certain number of twigs will become a branch, a certain amount of scrap metal will become a lump of metal you can use to rebuild something, and so on and so on.  This allows you to help rebuild your camp into more of a city and give you a better head-start on your next trek into the unknown.

Oh and don't be too concerned with how you place those tiles because every time you start out on the next expedition, the whole thing is cleared and your loop may look entirely different.  Not only that but you might find you are going counter-clockwise instead of clockwise.  Pretty much everything except for what you take to camp is blown away and you start again next go-round.  

Enemies ramp up in difficulty the more "loops" you make and for me I found that 6 or 7 was about the most I could make without needing to return to camp for heals and to try to build something.  There's really nothing that forces you to place those cards down though, so you could potentially just run loops around nothing and fighting slimes the whole time.  In fact it might benefit you to do this as you can turn the unused cards into materials later.  Same for any unused weapons or armor.  After you build up a certain amount (12?) the excess is converted to materials and sent to your backpack. 

Of course placing the cards gets you more materials as you place them and/or whenever you pass the tiles on a loop.  Other tiles just add to the amount of healing you get each day (which doesn't correspond to one loop, so you may find that you hit 5 days per loop or more).  There's some strategy to how and what you place and it feels like one of those fancy card games where people are flipping over trap cards and tapping them for mana or whatever, but it's not nearly as complicated.

So yeah, the first few hours are pretty engaging as you find out more of the story which gets revealed in parts, but the dopamine rush starts to die off quickly (at least for me) and so after a while it's just left feeling "meh".   A little more skinner-box would make me keep playing, or a little more story (which could have been told a bit better) but I got this game on sale so I'm not really complaining.  I just don't see myself spending a lot of time on this game.  It feels like I could be doing something better.

Loop hero has you go on expeditions to try to recover the world from the void that engulfed it. It features some of the most unique pixel art I've seen, really leaning into a 90's dark fantasy style. As you go on expeditions, you collect resources to grow your home camp. While on an expedition, your character fights monsters automatically. The only actions you take as the player are placing terrain cards you get from enemies, equipping newly acquired gear and returning to camp when the time is right.

For me, Loop Hero was a very hand-off experience. Yet it was curiously engaging, with me wanting to progress the story, expand my camp and discover more of what the game had to offer. After about 40 hours and collecting all achievements, I do have some things to say.

Gameplay is incredibly unique. Despite its passive nature, you do feel connected to the path your hero takes and the enemies they encounter. There is a dialogue system in the game that introduces you to a wide range of characters (including monsters!). The story interested me in that I wanted to know how this story would end - how would the world come back after being swallowed by the void?

Playing terrain tiles and equipping new gear served for pretty tight moment-to-moment gameplay. You look forward to beating enemies to see what juicy rewards you recieve. And then there is the fact that every loop could be your last. If you die during the expedition, you lose 70% of your resource. Abandon the expedition too far from the camp, and you lose 40%. Only if you are on the camp itself do you return will all resources. This led to good tension, me thinking if I could do another loop and being mad at myself when another loops goes awry. Because at the core of the game lays the camp. As it grows larger, you grow stronger. And building new structures and upgrading them was very satisfying, with the added bonus of getting more dialogue sequences at times.

I do have criticisms. I believe the synergy of certain tiles could have been expanded upon more - make me think more about my tile placement, punish me if I put tiles down in a stupid fashion. There really aren't any bad synergies, just unfortunate placement that can make your life harder. Additionally, I had to look up some synergies that I could not have thought of. More hints would have helped out there.

I also mentioned the story, It is interesting, there are a lot of characters whith unique dialogues, there is an encyclopedia that details what you have learned... but the ending [/spoiler]was meh, in my opinion. Maybe I did not get it, but it was pretty unsatisfying to me. I thought I would see the world bloom in its old glory, seeing the game's art style come to life fully on my screen, but no. The void persists.[/]

One thing I will admit is that I did cheese the game at times. You can alt f4 to get another chance at a battle, hoping RNGesus will roll the die in your favor. I am indifferent to this fact, though it did help me out at times.

I reccommend this game to people who want some laid-back but engaging roguelike gameplay. The game has a simple yet unique gameplay loop that can hook you in, and building out you camp is very nice to do. But don't expect the greatest story. Get the game on a slight discount, as I do not think the price is completely justifed.

I wish I could give this a "eh, it's alright" rating rather than a thumbs up or thumbs down. I like the soundtrack, aesthetic, worldbuilding, and concept far more than the execution of the actual strategy game. There's so much the game does well (mostly its music), but ultimately I had a hard time enjoying its very repetitive and grindy gameplay loop. In so many ways, I wish this game wasn't a roguelite but a pure roguelike: the grinding for progression drags the entire thing down. I often wondered if my strategy was incorrect, or if I simply hadn't grinded enough. I'm sure there are ways to do well without 30+ hrs of grinding if you know what you're doing, but good luck finding them. What's more likely is you'll probably spend a bunch of runs doing pretty much the same thing just to farm resources. And the game just isn't that fun when that's all you're doing. If every run was different and you could explore tons of varied builds while grinding, that'd be one thing, but there isn't much room for experimentation here (especially when you haven't unlocked everything).

Which is odd to say because the concept lends itself to a lot of neat ideas. You're playing an autobattler where you control the map and the equipment of your hero. Sort of like an idle game, except, well you can't really leave it idle. But so many of the tiles and choices the game gives you just aren't all that interesting? You'll first have the confusion of trying to understand the game's myriad of gameplay systems, then maybe try this or that out, only to find that most of the options it gives you aren't viable. Which leaves you with finding the rather boring optimal strategy that nearly everyone lands on ([spoiler]Thickets with rivers[/spoiler]). A strategy mind you, which IS THE SAME on all 3 of the game's classes. I once heard someone remark "oh your playstyle is just like mine! I do that too!" and I wanted to scream "yeah, that's what everyone does." Once you mercilessly grind the game to a pulp, more options open up and you can do more but at that point you can beat the final boss with just about anything and it becomes more of a challenge to see how long you can last. Which is, fine, I suppose, but I don't know it feels rather cheap? How am I supposed to engage with the strategy of the game for the first 30 or so hours when I know it will all be irrelevant once I've grinded enough? Am I supposed to feel like a master strategist for trivializing the game with extreme grinding?

The loop layout is different each run, which you'd think would drastically change your playstyle, but not really. You go in with a build idea and execute it. You don't really need to improvise or think all that hard. The classes aren't even very different. The most interesting decision in the game is how bosses are spawned; the game has an ingenious mechanic where the more tiles you place, the closer you get to spawning a boss at the end of your current loop. So you have to decide whether to pace your build out or continue developing your map. Cool, awesome mechanic. Once you play the game a bunch it becomes one of the few things you're making decisions around during a run. I wish there were like 5 or 6 other ideas like this mixed into the strategy here. To be clear, I'm not asking for more complexity, as there is a lot of it here. Rather, I'd like for all that complexity to actually produce something dynamic and interesting, which with the exception of the aforementioned mechanic, and a handful of other things (finding the optimal pathing for a river was cool, not that it matters), I didn't feel it did. How you have to beat the first boss was neat, though. Wish the other 3 had you work around their design in a similarly engaging way.

There are only 4 chapters, but I'd consider the first 3 tutorials compared to the final chapter. It will take you ~12 hours to do the first 3, and probably ~20 more to do the final one. You can see the steep dropoff in the achievements ... only 3.4% of players actually beat chapter 4. I wouldn't say that's because it's particularly hard or anything, but rather that it takes a ton of grinding. I did it with all 3 characters, without guides or outside help, but honestly I'm not sure if it was worth it. I'd feel a lot more proud of it if I felt like I made some great decisions or whatever, but that's really not what happened. I think it would have certainly been less grindy and much simpler had I simply looked up strategies ... but in a game with no mechanical skill, I'm not sure the point of playing anymore had I done that. Having said that, now that my save file is fully grinded to death, it's actually quite hard to lose (to the bosses at least). So, yeah, if you grind enough everything gets trivialized very quickly.

There's a lot of obtuseness to the mechanics too; you really have no way of knowing what each stat does without looking it up, but if you do you'll end up borrowing strategies from what you read, which cheapens what is already a pretty cheapened completion, what with all the grinding. Like, how am I supposed to know "Defense" is nearly useless? "Regen per second" sounds like an incredible stat, right? Guess what, it's actually hot garbage. And for Necromancer "Skeleton Level" is the god of all stats, but "Summon Quality" matters much less? Would be great if this stuff was broken down better in-game. The fact that stats are so uneven has a knock-on effect of making the game have extreme variance. You'll play the exact same way, with the same build, and in one run you'll die on loop 6 and in the other you'll make it to loop 20. Not because you made better choices or anything, but because the items that dropped in the loop 20 run happened to have the actual important stats and not the useless ones. With the grinding, randomness, autobattling, and lack of decision making, you start to wonder if you're even the one playing, or if the game is just playing itself. This variance makes it exceptionally hard to pin down how to optimize; who's to say your last run went well because of a card you added or because you got lucky with an item or trait at a key time?

Given all that, why am I so reluctant to give this game a thumbs down? Well, because it tried. It tried really hard. The music is excellent (I know I've said this 3 times now but it's that good), the core design is rock solid and unique, the story and characters are engaging but not overbearing, and the artstyle fits the game wonderfully. Battle animations are great, with a great variety of enemies. There's a wonderful encyclopedia in-game which though its much more for lore than it is for mechanics (you'll need a wiki for that), is still well-done overall. And frankly there is something very cool about having your well-oiled loop running in harmony; the core idea is awesome and doesn't get old. 

So that is all to say that I want more games like this, and I'd play their next game. There's a lot of love put into Loop Hero. I didn't connect with it much, but I applaud the effort.

If you played the demo for the game you've basically seen all the full game has to offer. Very little changes, expands, or improves. There are a few new cards, a few new buildings, and a few new classes. And that's it. A bunch of people have posted reviews saying: "I got x amount of hours from the demo!" Well that's because the demo shows the entire hand of the full game. 

The general gameplay of the game consists mostly of staring at the screen while your hero battles at a snails pace, then sorting through what's usually a bunch of trash loot in hopes that something you got is an upgrade. Then you slap down some tiles to the map and repeat. 

Speaking of which, placing tiles on the map becomes really mundane after a while because you know where everything should go, and there isn't a whole lot of thought process there. You don't get a lot of meaningful choices in how to build the map (or your deck thanks to the limited amount of total cards). I was really hoping that there would be a whole lot more tile combo's where placing certain tiles adjacent to another would create new, interesting modifiers, but there is very little of that.  Instead you get to slap a river down and some forests next to it across half the map and call it a day.

Aside from that, you get to upgrade your town in between expeditions, which is a massive grind for gains that are generally questionable at best. Hope you like games of a very repetitive nature, because this one has repetition in spades. 

Finally, the game's balance constantly left me astonished at how poor it felt at times. Everything from bosses, classes, cards and monster's could probably use a whole lot of buffs/nerfs or tweaks. Take one of the rogue's level-up upgrades for instance: it gives you 3 hp back per kill. 3 hp, when mobs start hitting for upwards of 60 damage a swing. Seemsgood. And another example, the last boss in the game simply deletes one of your equipped items or stats. In a combat system where you have ZERO control in a fight and can only tweak your equipment, that is the dumbest design of a boss I've seen, somewhat akin to Risk of Rain's 2 final boss who also removed all your gear.

So yeah. I'm kind of baffled how everyone is raving about how good this game is. I'd say it's massively overrated right now. Sure, it's cheap, and if you buy it and turn your brain off, you'll probably have some fun. But if you like deep strategy games, interesting deck builders, or robust combat systems, you're best off looking elsewhere.

There's no denying that this game is ffffiiiiiine? It's fine, it's well-priced, but you'll pay with your time rather than your wallet, and be left feeling like you wasted most of it. I've no idea why it took off as hard as it did: it's got lovely visuals and a great moody soundtrack, but its entire premise is barely built upon, and instead stretched out into monotony.

So you have a lil guy who walks around a pre-built path in a loop and you place objects around in each others' proximity to create enemies and loot and whatnot for them to pick up. It's a good idea for an almost-idle game, but chapter 1 is the same as chapter 4, and the bonuses you get from placing anything other than monster spawners is just negligible.

It sounds lovely, the idea of building a landscape in a void out of a hand of cards, improvising as you go, but none of it really does anything, other than increase your health by 1 point, taking you from 2098 to 2099, or giving you 23 health per day instead of 22. The persistent town building is exactly the same, meaning what is meant to be the big reward for your grinding away is instead just kind of mandatory to progress, but wishy washy and minor. So the aesthetic board building aspect is gone, so is the pay-off with the city building, fine, I guess that's not what they were going for. But what about monsters? Gameplay? Well, there aren't very many types, and their numbers just go up the longer you play. Well... loot? Nope, maybe 5 or 6 sets that don't really work well with one another, so you sit there waiting for a full vampirism set or riposte or whatever, basically just playing snap with the game.

As I said, chapter 1 = chapter 4: you place things as you get them, concentrate it all on the bendiest section of the loop, and watch it unfold. You can't quite switch off though, or you'll die, so you have to keep swapping out equipment, arbitrarily switching out builds depending on what drops. It's not really satisfying; there's very little strategy, which would work as a minimalistic idle game, but this falls somewhere in between where it just ended up feeling like a lacklustre chore with great ambience. By the end I was running the game in 10x speed and wanting it over just because I'd already sunk a bit of time into it.

It's fine, I'm just not sure what it was meant to be, nor why it's been spoken about so much: I finished it and wouldn't recommend it to anyone, because it's not quite easy or simple enough to be a fun throwaway afternoon mobile game, but nor is it any more engaging than your average skinner box.

Expertly combines simple but effect parts of various games such as deck-builders, tile/city building, auto-battler, and rouge-lite into an odd but smooth and satisfying experience. The variety of ways you can play any one run combined with the desire of completing "just one more loop" makes it really engaging. Finally, the well done retro-style graphics and music brings it all together as a fun and very unique game. Highly recommended!
